title: Oryx Eyes Between al-Rusafa and the Bridge
intro: Ali ibn al-Jahm wrote this in praise of the caliph al-Mutawakkil, whom it calls by his own name, Ja'far; it mentions the three sons he made his heirs, which al-Tabari dates to 235 AH (850 CE), so the poem comes after. It opens on the women of Baghdad between al-Rusafa and the bridge and turns to grey hair and the end of youth; then it becomes a scene in which the poet overhears two women talking about him and answers that he is no poet living by his verses, but a man whose name makes his verses travel. From there it moves to the caliph, his generosity and piety, and the glory of the Abbasid house. Khalil Mardam Bek at first found the poem only in pieces scattered through the literary books and gathered 43 abyat; he later found fuller texts, the last of 62 abyat from al-Shayzari's Jamharat al-Islam, which the recitation follows, and called it al-Rusafiyya. Writers, Mardam notes, loved to quote its opening line and wove stories around it; in one, told by Ibn Arabi in Muhadarat al-abrar, the poet arrives at court a rough Bedouin whom Baghdad made tender, a story Mardam calls fanciful.

translation: Oryx eyes between al-Rusafa and the bridge
have brought me love by ways I know and ways I don't.
1.sharh: Women's glances on a Baghdad street bring love on him, some he noticed and some he didn't.

translation: They brought back my old longing, though I had
never got over it: they heaped embers on embers.
2.sharh: There was nothing to bring back: the old love was still burning, and they added to the fire.

translation: They came away unhurt and left hearts to ruin,
as if pierced by the tips of straight brown spears.
3.sharh: Salimna wa-aslamna, “they were safe and they abandoned”, plays on one root: the women escape love untouched while the hearts they look at are speared.

translation: They told us, “We are new moons: we only
light the night traveller's way, and offer him no food.”
4.sharh: Their beauty is for looking at, like moonlight: it shows the way but feeds no one. Feeding a traveller was the first duty of desert hospitality.

translation: No gift but what an eye takes away for the road,
no union but with the phantom that comes by night.
5.sharh: All a lover gets is a look to remember and the beloved's image in his dreams.

translation: Just when they had shaken my heart from its place
and set fire to all between my ribs and breast,
6.sharh: The thought runs on into the next line: he cannot believe they turned away at that moment of all moments.

translation: they turned away, as a drinker turns from wine
once he has had his fill, for fear of getting drunk.
7.sharh: They withdraw like a careful drinker who stops before he loses his head, as if they feared falling in love themselves.

translation: Why did they not, before grey hair showed, start me
on plain despair, or turn to betrayal then?
8.sharh: His complaint is about timing: if they were going to give him up, they might have done it while he was still young.

translation: If they have changed, or denied a pledge they gave,
that is nothing new or strange in beautiful women.
9.sharh: Fickleness is the old charge against the beloved in Arabic love poetry; he makes it a commonplace, nothing to wonder at.

translation: But youth has perished, and oryx
are hunted only with youth and wealth.
10.sharh: The real reason is plain: he is no longer young, and beauty, like game, is caught only with youth and money.

translation: Love is occupation enough, and grey hair warning enough,
if love were a thing that warnings held back.
11.sharh: Grey hair ought to end a man's love affairs, but love does not listen.

translation: Yet, by the grey hair that frightened them, many a time
their fingertips pressed me from breast to throat.
12.sharh: He swears by the very grey hair that drove them off: before it, they embraced him.

translation: We spent the night together in spite of the slanderers,
blended like rain from the clouds and wine.
13.sharh: Wine was drunk mixed with water, and rainwater was the purest; the lovers are as inseparable as the two in the cup.

translation: My two friends, how sweet love is, and how bitter,
and how well I know its sweetness and its bitterness.
14.sharh: Poets traditionally address two companions. He speaks as a man who has tasted both sides of love.

translation: By the bond between us, have you ever seen
anything gentler than complaint, or harsher than desertion,
15.sharh: He sets the two extremes of love side by side: the lover's soft complaint and the beloved's hard rejection.

translation: or anything that betrays a lover's secret like his eye,
above all when it lets a tear run free?
16.sharh: A lover may keep silent, but his eyes give him away.

translation: Whatever I forget, I will never forget her saying
to her friend, “How love clings to the noble!”
17.sharh: From here the poem becomes a scene: he overhears two women talking about him.

translation: The other said to her, “Then why is our friend
in torment? Have you any excuse for killing him?”
18.sharh: The second woman pleads his case; he is “our friend” to both.

translation: “Be kind to him: union may bring him back to life;
and know that love's captive is the worst bound of all.”
19.sharh: Love as captivity is an old image; she argues it is worse than any other.

translation: She said, “I must hide him from people, and love
is seldom sweet but to one who tears the veil away.”
20.sharh: She loves him, she implies, but must keep it hidden, and hidden love has little sweetness.

translation: Then both were sure I had heard, and said,
“Who is this caller in the night, listening unseen?”
21.sharh: He has been listening all along; the women only now notice him.

translation: I said, “A young man who, if you wish, keeps love secret;
if not, one who throws off rein and bridle.”
22.sharh: He offers them discretion, or else open scandal.

translation: “Though he complains of a cruel one who grudges him
even a smiling greeting and a cheerful face.”
23.sharh: He speaks of himself in the third person, as the women did.

translation: She said, “We have been lampooned!” I said, “Some of what you say
is true: perhaps one evil wards off another.”
24.sharh: She takes his complaint for satire. He half admits it, as a fair answer to their cruelty.

translation: She said, “I can see the rhymes already, travelling
with us from city to city.”
25.sharh: She fears his verses will carry their story everywhere.

translation: I said, “You think ill of me: I am no poet,
though at times my breast will well over with verse.”
26.sharh: The denial is half a joke, made in verse. It leads into what follows: he is a man of rank, not a poet who lives by his poems.

translation: “Be kind, and ask anyone you like: they will tell you
that, come what may, I am the best keeper of a secret.”
27.sharh: His reputation for discretion is meant to calm her fear of the poems.

translation: I am not one whose name was made by his poems:
it is my name that sends my poems on their way.
28.sharh: He is still answering her. He reverses the usual order: his standing makes his verses famous, not the other way round.

translation: Poetry is no shade I shelter in;
it has neither raised my standing nor lowered it.
29.sharh: Ibn Rashiq explains: poetry did not raise him, because he was a man of note before he wrote it, and did not lower him, because it is no disgrace in itself and he made it only for the caliph.

translation: Poetry has many followers, but I have never
been one of them, in hard times or in easy.
30.sharh: Professional poets lived on the gifts their praise earned; he sets himself apart from them.

translation: Not everyone who leads horses can manage them,
nor is everyone who races one a horseman.
31.sharh: So not everyone who makes verses is a poet: he composes, but does not make a trade of it.

translation: But the kindness of the caliph Ja'far
is what moved me to the verses I made about him,
32.sharh: Here the poem turns to praise. Ibn Rashiq admired the move: the poet presents his praise as a return for kindness, not as a plea for reward.

translation: and they have travelled like the sun to every land,
and blown like the wind over land and sea.
33.sharh: Having denied being a poet, he boasts of how far his poems have gone, the very thing the woman feared.

translation: If any giver were too great to be thanked for his favour,
the Commander of the Faithful would be too great for thanks.
34.sharh: No thanks could match the caliph's gifts.

translation: A young man whose face gladdens the eyes
as his flood of giving gladdens the hands.
35.sharh: Eyes and hands are both made happy: the one by his face, the other by his gifts.

translation: Through him Islam was kept safe from every heretic,
and a back-breaking blow fell on those who strayed.
36.sharh: Shawqi Dayf reads this as praise of al-Mutawakkil's stand against the Mu'tazila, after the inquisition over the createdness of the Quran.

translation: An imam of right guidance, who cleared the faith of its troubles
after the factions of unbelief had fallen on its followers.
37.sharh: The caliph is presented as the restorer of religion after a time of strife.

translation: The bounty of his right hand scattered his wealth,
and yet it left him the finest name.
38.sharh: Money goes, praise stays: the old exchange at the heart of Arabic ideas of generosity.

translation: What could anyone praising him achieve, even if he were
Zuhayr, and al-A'sha, and Imru' al-Qays son of Hujr?
39.sharh: He names three of the greatest pre-Islamic poets: together they could not praise him enough.

translation: When we liken him to the full moon rising
and to the sun, people say the sun and moon are honoured.
40.sharh: The usual compliment is reversed: the honour is the sun's and the moon's for being compared with him.

translation: Whoever says that the sea and the rain resemble
his generosity has paid the sea and the rain a compliment.
41.sharh: The sea and the rain were the stock images of a generous ruler; here they are flattered by the comparison.

translation: And if Ja'far has come to rely on God
in private and in public,
42.sharh: A play on his title: al-Mutawakkil means “the one who relies on God”. In the fuller text the sentence ends in a line the reciter leaves out: “God has rewarded the caliph Ja'far”.

translation: and has made three heirs over the Muslims,
hailed with support, and might, and victory,
43.sharh: Al-Mutawakkil named three sons his heirs: al-Muntasir, al-Mu'tazz and al-Mu'ayyad. The three blessings echo their titles: ta'yid, support, for al-Mu'ayyad; izz, might, for al-Mu'tazz; nasr, victory, for al-Muntasir.

translation: Do you want any witness but God's Book
to your glory and honour, sons of al-Abbas?
44.sharh: The next two lines cite the Quran itself as that witness.

translation: It is enough that God has entrusted His affairs to you,
and revealed, “Obey those in authority.”
45.sharh: He quotes the Quran (4:59), “Obey God, obey the Messenger and those in authority among you”, as proof of the caliphs' right.

translation: The Prophet Muhammad asked no other reward of people
than love for his close kin.
46.sharh: Another Quranic allusion (42:23), “I ask you no reward for it except love for kin”, read as a command to love the Prophet's family, to which the Abbasids belonged.

translation: If others' homes are unknown, yours
lie between al-Hajun and al-Hijr.
47.sharh: Their homes are in Mecca itself, from the hill above the city down to the Kaaba.

translation: God's House has always stood among your houses,
defended by you with keen Indian swords.
48.sharh: The Abbasids descend from the clan of Hashim, who watered and fed the pilgrims before Islam.

translation: The faces of the sons of al-Abbas adorn kingship
as the bright stars adorn the heavens.
49.sharh: The dynasty is to the caliphate what the stars are to the sky.

translation: Kingship dawns only with those it belongs to,
as days come round only to the month.
50.sharh: Istahalla, “to dawn”, is used of the new moon that starts a month, which ties the two halves together: the caliphate begins with the Abbasids as surely as each month begins with its moon.

translation: So greet the sons of al-Abbas from me with a greeting
that will travel down the days, sweet-scented.
51.sharh: The greeting is the poem itself.

translation: Recited, it will add to your loyal friend's joy,
and be a back-breaking blow to those who stray.
52.sharh: He turns to the caliph for the last line, which echoes the end of line 36.

1.1.2.meaning: Maha: oryx, the wild cow of the desert; its large dark eyes are the poets' image for a woman's.

1.1.4.head: الرُّصافة
1.1.4.meaning: Al-Rusafa: a quarter on the east bank of Baghdad.

1.1.5.head: الجِسر
1.1.5.meaning: The bridge over the Tigris joining the two halves of Baghdad.

3.2.3-4.head: المُثَقَّفَة السُّمر
3.2.3-4.meaning: “The straightened brown ones”: spears of dark cane, trued straight.

4.2.6.head: قَرى
4.2.6.meaning: Naqri: we give food to a guest; qira is the meal owed to a traveller.

5.2.4.head: الخَيال
5.2.4.meaning: Khayal: the beloved's phantom, which visits a lover in sleep.

9.2.3.head: الغَواني
9.2.3.meaning: Ghawani: beautiful women; literally, those whose beauty needs no ornament.

11.2.1-2.head: لَو أَنَّ
11.2.1-2.meaning: Law-anna, “if”: the hamza is dropped and its vowel moved back, as the metre needs.

12.2.4.head: سَحر
12.2.4.meaning: Sahr: the lungs; here, the upper chest.

13.1.4.head: الوُشاة
13.1.4.meaning: Wushat: slanderers, the gossips who work to part lovers, a stock figure of love poetry.

14.1.1.head: خَليل
14.1.1.meaning: “My two friends”: poets traditionally address a pair of companions.

17.1.3.head: مِن
17.1.3.meaning: Mi-l-ashya', “of things”: min, “of”, shortened before the article.

21.2.2.head: الطّارِق
21.2.2.meaning: Tariq: one who comes knocking by night.

22.2.2-4.head: خَلّاع الأَعِنَّة وَالعُذر
22.2.2-4.meaning: “Shedder of reins and cheek-straps”: one who has thrown off all restraint, like a horse without a halter.

25.2.3.head: مِصر
25.2.3.meaning: Misr: a city; also the name of Egypt.

32.1.4.head: جَعفَر
32.1.4.meaning: Ja'far: the caliph al-Mutawakkil, who reigned 232–247 AH (847–861 CE).

39.2.1.meaning: Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma, pre-Islamic poet, famous for his wisdom.

39.2.2.head: الأَعشى
39.2.2.meaning: Al-A'sha, Maymun ibn Qays, pre-Islamic poet of praise and wine.

39.2.3-6.head: اِمرُؤُ القَيس
39.2.3-6.meaning: Imru' al-Qays son of Hujr, of Kinda, the most famous of the pre-Islamic poets.

42.1.5.head: مُتَوَكِّل
42.1.5.meaning: Mutawakkil: relying on God; also the caliph's title, al-Mutawakkil ala Allah.

44.2.3-4.head: بَنو العَبّاس
44.2.3-4.meaning: Banu al-Abbas: the Abbasid dynasty, descended from al-Abbas, the Prophet's uncle.

47.2.3.head: الحَجون
47.2.3.meaning: Al-Hajun: a hill at the upper end of Mecca.

47.2.5.head: الحِجر
47.2.5.meaning: Al-Hijr: the low walled space beside the Kaaba.

48.2.3.head: المُهَنَّدة
48.2.3.meaning: Muhannada: swords of Indian steel, the finest.
